speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I share the opinion
which has been expressed by the exiled member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) who is on this side of the chamber, in complimenting and congratulating the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie (Mr. Raymond) upon having brought this matter before the house, and especially upon the extremely impressive speech with which he supported this bill when he introduced it some weeks ago. In a way it is a pity that these public bills moved by hon. members come only at very considerable intervals, and that we are likely to lose sight of them from one week to another until they spring up again at a time when the session is nearing its end and it is not always possible to give them the consideration which some of them deserve. I am glad, however, to see that this bill has been called early tonight; and perhaps the house will permit me, while expressing my opinions on the different sections of the bill, to make sure that my speech is over before nine o'clock, so that at least so far as I am concerned I shall not stand in the way of the house expressing its opinion in the matter.
I said that the hon. member for Beau-harnois supported this bill in a very able way. Perhaps I should qualify that statement and say that he presented the house with a picture of conditions in the textile industry which, I am sure, immensely impressed the house, and also the people, if I may judge from editorials published in certain newspapers. But there is one thing which he has not done. He has not discussed the bill itself. In other words he has vividly depicted the evil he wants to cure, but he has not discussed the remedy which he proposes, and it is my ungrateful task to submit

to the house to-night, to the best of my ability, that the bill, at least in its present form, will hardly meet the requirements, and to suggest that if the house gives it second reading it should be amended considerably before it goes on the statute book.
The object of the bill, as expressed in the explanatory notes, is:
... to amend The Companies Act ... so as to enable the Secretary of State to obtain information on the business and management of the industries afforded protection under the customs tariff, with a view to having control over the profits of such companies and over the payment of dividends, and also with a view to ascertaining whether these companies fulfil their obligations with respect to their employees and the public.
I may have time during the course of my remarks to show that some of the information which it is sought to obtain through this bill is already furnished to the government through other departments, if not the Secretary of State's department. But that is not the main point.
As far as the bill would merely impose upon the companies the obligation of filing with the Secretary of State the very fullest statement as to their business, I wrould not offer the least objection to it. I do not think that I would even consider objecting to section 4, which asks for extended information as to the wages paid to the working men, the hours of work, and all that concerns the labour element in the industry. I believe that there can be no objection at all, even from a constitutional point of view, to the filing of such information with the Secretary of State. But when the Secretary of State is asked to take that information into account in order to form an opinion as to whether a company shall or shall not pay a dividend, it is a different matter. In other words, the Secretary of State is asked not only to gather information as to the operations of the company, the hours of work and the wages paid, but also to express his opinion as to whether these wages are sufficient, as to whether the working conditions are proper, and, according to the way he thinks about these matters, to consent or to withhold his consent to the payment by the company of its regular dividends. Here we should be entering a hazardous field, from the purely constitutional point of view. I took the stand-and I believe the hon. member, who has been discussing this bill with me on several occasions and has shown a splendid spirit of cooperation in every way, for which I wish to pay him credit, agrees with me- that it would be primarily for the provinces to say whether proper wages are being paid to

Companies Act
working men in the different industries, and in a general way to supervise the working conditions of those industries.
But my main remarks must bear on the first section of the bill, which is the essential one. I will read it; it is not very long. The proposed new section, 83A, is set out as follows:
No public company manufacturing or making goods protected in whole or in part by the customs tariff may declare and pay dividends until the return or summary required under section one hundred and twenty-one of this act has been submitted to the Secretary of State-
That is the section which calls for additional information, including all the information concerning the wages and working conditions in the industry. Section 83A says further:
-and until the written consent of the Secretary of State as to such declaration and payment of dividends has been obtained.
In other words, the bill proposes to vest in the Secretary of State the authority either to consent to the declaration of dividends or to withhold that consent with respect to all companies enjoying tariff protection, and the bill does not even define what is meant by tariff protection. I do not know what amendments may be suggested in that regard, but as it stands it would mean that if the bill were accepted, no company enjoying the smallest degree of tariff protection could declare a dividend unless the Secretary of State gave his consent to such declaration.
Now I am a very modest man, and I say that this is an authority which no secretary of state should look for, and if any secretary of state ever sought it, no parliament should grant it. It would constitute such an authority over the conduct of industry throughout the country that parliament will readily see the danger of placing in the hands of one minister, however able or scrupulous he might be, so powerful a weapon. But, further, I submit that no secretary of state could discharge the duties involved in this proposal in a manner that would be satisfactory to parliament and to the public. This bill would impose upon the minister in charge of the department the novel and onerous responsibility of consenting to the payment of dividends. I have here a letter from a prominent lawyer whose opinion I sought in the matter, and who writes me to the effect that this bill practically takes away from the directors the management of any company making goods which are protected, and transfers it to the Secretary of State. When the Secretary of State is given, in addition to the information already called for by section 121, the further information
called for by the bill, he will have to consider, as to each company every year, the question of the fairness of its salaries, from the president downwards, its conditions of labour, its dividends in view of salaries, earnings, capital originally invested and so on. In other words, he will have to do every year for all these companies the work which it took the Turgeon commission months to do for the textile companies.
In the event of the Secretary of State withholding his written consent to the declaration and payment of dividends upon scrutiny of the return showing the list of employees and workers, the individual hours of work and the total amount of salary or wages received by each of them, each company with respect to which such consent was withheld" would demand the right to be heard and to submit further information calculated to justify, from their point of view, the desired declaration of a dividend and the sufficiency of the wages paid and of the hours of rest consistently with a great many factors such as capital investment, competitive conditions in the particular industry, seasonal fluctuations, world trade conditions and many other matters. Not only would a very large clerical staff be required to scrutinize and tabulate the information filed with the Secretary of State under the proposed amendment to section 121 of the Companies Act, but trained legal and other technical assistants, varying with the different industries under consideration, would have to be available for the assistance of the minister in considering and deciding upon individual cases in dispute.
Approximately 10,000 companies incorporated under the Companies Act (Canada) file returns with the Secretary of State annually under section 121 of the statute. Assuming that only one-half of these companies were engaged in manufacturing or making goods protected in whole or in part by the customs tariff, it must be borne in mind that many will employ hundreds, some even thousands, of individuals with varying hours of work and salary or wages.
In this connection it is interesting to observe that the proceedings of the Turgeon commission are recorded in many volumes, but I will not press that point. It is brought out in the letter I have read. After I had made known these objections to the mover of the bill he was perfectly willing to amend it so as not to have it apply to all of these companies, but rather to vest in the Secretary of State the power of intervening in exceptional cases. I may add that, in fact, he was quite prepared to suggest amendments to his own bill. I give him credit for that, and if I
Companies Act

have endeavoured to show why the bill in its original form is not acceptable I have a purpose in view. That purpose I trust I shall be permitted to intimate to the house.
Twice a week bills are moved in the house by members whose purposes are often highly commendable; but, if I may say so, the technical structure of such bills is not always acceptable and we ministers have the thankless task of rising in the house and trying to explain, not that we are opposed to the objects of the bill, but that the bill is not so drafted as to attain those objects. I put it to you. Mr. Speaker, if instead of dealing with the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie who has shown a conciliatory spirit and a willingness to cooperate, I had to deal with a stubborn member who insisted upon the original wording of the bill, I should have to stand here opposing the bill for technical reasons which I might regard as quite proper; and yet I would be denounced in certain sections of the press as being against the working man and unwilling to try to put through legislation to remedy certain evils. This happened not long ago. I am not permitted to refer at length to another bill that has been before the house, but I may say in passing that what I have just suggested has happened. Members have certain objects in view and it is perfectly proper that they should bring them to the attention of the house, whether the bills embodying those objects relate to the French language or to any other matter. But when we come here in good faith, with exactly the same desire that private members have to further the interests they have at heart, why should not we too be given credit for that good faith by the friends of hon. members and by those sections of the press that support them? When you pursue a certain object, surely it is only right to see that you do not put upon the statute book bills that are obviously not acceptable.
Coming back to the present bill, I may say that the mover has made it clear that he does not wish to place in the hands of the Secretary of State full control over every company enjoying tariff protection, but he wants to have the Secretary of State furnished with all the requisite information on which to base a decision in individual cases, and to see that in exceptional cases the Secretary of State shall be in a position to take action. That is a vastly different proposal from what was originally set out in the bill. The house has shown a pronounced inclination to favour the bill, not so much on account of its specific provisions as on account of its principle, so that I am quite willing to let 
the house decide. Personally I would not oppose the second reading, but it would be on the distinct understanding that the bill will have to be materially amended when it reaches the committee. I may even say that it had been my intention, if the bill had come earlier, to have it referred to a select committee of the house, preferably the committee on banking and commerce, but we all know that that committee is very busy now and I do not think it would help to have it referred to that committee. We should rather try and work it out in committee of the whole house.
There are a couple of other points that I desire to make very briefly. Much of the information called for by the bill is already available, either in the bureau of statistics or in the departments of labour or of trade and commerce. I see no objection-on the contrary there might be an advantage doing so-to grouping that information and having it available in the Department of State. But again I point to the fact that, from the constitutional point of view, when we come to deal with wages, not only in securing information but in taking action upon the information gathered, we are wandering in a dangerous field. Not being a lawyer I have a certain sympathy with the opinion expressed in this house on several occasions by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) that we should not always be blocked in our efforts to improve social conditions by finely drawn interpretations of constitutional nuances or difficulties. At the same time, if we legislate on a matter such as this, and, following the legislation, the Secretary of State feels called upon to interfere with the declaration of a dividend by a certain company, the company may appeal to the supreme court or to the privy council, and the point of view then taken will have to be a strictly legal one. The fact that we desired to improve social conditions would not stand against the strictly legal argument, as I understand the situation. But that is a matter which might be considered later.
We should be very careful in another direction. Companies may be incorporated either by the federal government or by the different provinces. I am not disclosing any secret when I say that there has always been a certain spirit of competition between federal and provincial authorities in this regard. It has been my own experience that very often when those desiring to incorporate a company come before the officers of my department to obtain certain concessions, and fail to obtain them, they at once repair to one of the provincial governments and obtain incorporation there. If

Companies Act
you impose too heavy obligations on companies you will merely achieve the end of reducing gradually the number which come to the federal department for incorporation. In an effort to avoid that, and I think in a very good spirit, in recent years representatives of the different provincial governments, especially from the departments of the attorneys general, have met with my own officers in an attempt to realize what may be the millennial hope of securing uniformity in the federal and provincial companies acts in this country. They are working on that now. I have myself attended several meetings, and, having practically agreed that we should not materially amend the different companies acts either in the provinces or the dominion, it would be with a certain reluctance that I should see the federal act amended in any material way.
If there were not two sides to a question it would not be worth while discussing it. At the same time I appreciate that if conditions are such as the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie has indicated, it is up to this parliament to do something. But since the working men themselves have expressed their desire not to recommend any material decrease in the tariff for fear the factories might close and they might lose their jobs, and since from all appearances the provincial government concerned has not acted to improve the labour conditions in the industry to which reference has been made, personally I will not stand between the evil and a certain degree of remedy. Therefore, although I believe the situation is fraught with difficulty I will not object to second reading of the bill, with the distinct understanding that when it is considered in committee we shall have to examine it very carefully and make material changes.

On what basis are the allotments made?
The number of pilots trained. A grant of $100 is made for each private licence issued and so much an hour for a commercial licence.
Is it felt that value is being received for these grants?

Yes, I think so. There has been some sorting out of the clubs. At one time some clubs were located in cities which really did not have a sufficient number of students to warrant their carrying on. But the number of clubs has been reduced, and I think the present clubs are amply justified. This is the only source of private training open to pilots desiring to enter commercial work. The only other training a man can obtain is to enter the militia, which involves signing up for a period of years. Private training is paid for privately; these grants are only to give assistance to the clubs.
Through the years these clubs have turned out a considerable number of commercial pilots. At the moment they are performing a very useful work in giving preliminary training and making a selection of pilots who wish to enter the air force. Instead of having to go to a military training centre, these students may take their course at the local club. If they are found qualified, they are sent on to the training camps.

I am pleased to hear the minister make the statement he just made. It seemed to me that these clubs offer an excellent training ground, not only for commercial pilots but for pilots of all types and classes. The amounts granted to some of these clubs are small compared with the usefulness of the service they render. These flying clubs are located all across the dominion; they are not limited to any one locality. They have turned out some excellent men. Unfortunately some of the clubs are located in districts where the interest has been comparatively light. I refer to the interest in the club, rather than to the number of pilots. Considering the difficulties which the Department of National Defence has been facing, it seems to me that here is an opportunity by which we can increase not only the interest in flying but the efficiency of our pilots. I think the minister might well give consideration to increasing this vote substantially. He has just stated he feels that full value is being received from what has been expended so far, and $35,000 distributed among twenty-two clubs does not seem a large amount of money. If the grant were doubled, perhaps it would double the efficiency of the work.

I doubt if the way to make these clubs efficient is to give them too much money. Some years ago many clubs were in a precarious financial position, but I am glad to say that to-day they are in a first-class financial position. This is mainly on account of the Canadian Flying Clubs Association which controls the different clubs. This association has had splendid officers at its head, and they have brought the equipment of the various clubs to a high state of efficiency. In my opinion the grants now provided are sufficient to keep the clubs in efficient operation provided there is proper management. For a number of years these clubs will receive considerable revenue from the Department of National Defence for performing certain work for that department.

I had in mind that the money would be used only for equipment and

Supply-Transport-Air Service
training and not to make the clubs more attractive in appearance or anything of that kind.
What equipment have the clubs obtained to date? Has that equipment been obtained out of their own resources, or have they used some of these grants to obtain training ships.

In the initial stages we gave each club two training planes, and subsequently one plane for each plane they bought. Recently we have been making no grants for equipment, simply the allowance for training, but I believe the clubs have all the equipment they need, and some have more than they can use to advantage.
It is a straight cash grant for the club?
Yes.
What is the number of pilots trained in the various clubs last year?
Since 1929 the clubs have graduated 1,721 private pilots and 423 commercial pilots. Last year the clubs turned out 230 private pilots and fifty commercial pilots.

I imagine the majority of
them have been trained in the last few years, have they not? After all, there was a serious depression from 1929 on for a few years.
Has the minister the number of pilots turned out each year in each of the provinces? I understand that in the province of Quebec there is only one club, that in Montreal.

Yes. Montreal last year
turned out six private pilots.
Out of how many training?
The membership in the club is 127, and the number under instruction, ten.
How many pilots were turned out in the whole dominion last year?
There were 230 last year.

I am of the same opinion as the hon. member for Greenwood. I think this department, in view of the progress made in aviation, should increase its estimate for that purpose. As a member coming from the province of Quebec I would be very much pleased if this were done, in consequence of which more people in the province of Quebec

would have facilities available to them for acquiring training as pilots. I am sure there is not more being done in the province of Quebec in that field. I am sure that the minister is as anxious as anyone to see an improvement in that field, and I repeat, I should like the Department of Transport to increase this estimate so that facilities may be at the disposal of our province and the country at large to obtain knowledge and training in aircraft.

1)06. To provide for contributions to assist municipalities to improve existing airports, or to provide new airports, and for direct construction works on municipal or government airports serving municipalities, the sites of which have been provided by such municipalities, $800,000.
How near completion is the Island airport at Toronto?

its. Canals service administration, $33,340.
I wanted to say something with reference to canals, and I wondered if the minister would object to my saying it under this item.
Go right ahead.

I shall take only a few moments, because I do not believe that under this item I should say much of what I have to say. Some few days ago-to be exact, on May 13-I asked a question of the government in reference to what action they were going to take with regard to the proposed opening of the sluice gates in the canal south of Long lake, between Long lake and lake Superior. I pointed out that there were at present some 50,000 cords of pulpwood on the ice in that lake, and that the Ontario government proposed shortly to open the canal. I assume that the Prime Minister should have replied to the question, but the minister

Supply-Transport-Canals Service
replied, and I rise merely to set him right on this subject, not to pass any particular comment on what he said. His reply was:
My information is that there is very serious flooding of the railway tracks in the vicinity of Longlac, where the line has been washed out twice.
As a matter of fact the line at Longlac has never been washed out at any time. During the spring there were two wash-outs east of Longlac, I believe near Seagram and Horne-payne, and west of Longlac, but the line at Longlac itself is so much higher than the water level that to wash out the line would mean the washing out of the buildings adjacent to Longlac station, and my information is that nothing of that kind has occurred at any time.

I am told that the water was
so dangerously high this spring at that particular point that on that account the gates were opened.

That had nothing to do with it. The gates are not opened yet. The water at no time was dangerous at Longlac station, and as I have said, the particular gales to which I have reference have not been opened yet. It is proposed to open them. These particular gates are south of the height of land and some six miles south of the south end of Long lake itself.
However, I give the minister the correct information. A day or two after asking my question of May 13, I asked the Prime Minister if there had been any action taken following the letter of the United States secretary of state of March 17, 1938. The Prime Minister replied:
I am unable to answer my hon. friend's question at the moment, but I shall try to see that an answer is given to-morrow.
On the following day, May 16, the Minister of Justice replied for the Prime Minister, saying:
Yesterday the hon. member for Davenport . . . asked a question of the Prime Minister ... to which he promised an answer to-day. The question is to be found on page 4334 of Hansard. The answer is, no; there have been no further developments.
The question was, whether any change had taken place between Canada and the United States as to permitting the opening of the gate in the canal south of Long lake, and the answer was, no. I merely wish to add that I know the minister gave his answer in good faith, but the information given to

him was incorrect so far as Longlac was concerned ; and if he wishes thoroughly to familiarize himself with the subject I would recommend that he study the two white papers given out by the Prime Minister last year. They tell the whole story. I have them here, but I am not going to take up time with them now. The matter will come up, I assume, under external affairs. The fact is that the line at Longlac has not been washed out; I am satisfied that the water would have to rise approximately eight feet before it could become a menace to the tracks, and I am informed that never in the history of Long lake has the water risen that high.

Has the minister any information with regard to under what right or under what lease or other agreement the Rideau Aquatic Club are located on the Rideau canal and have the slip, or whatever they call it, where they put their boats in. The reason I ask the question is that the condition there has been rather unsightly all spring, and is yet. I wondered if that will obtain there for all time. It is an unsatisfactory exhibition at the edge of a million dollar drive which belongs to the federal government.

The Rideau Aquatic Club
holds a lease from the Department of Transport. I am told that no complaint has been received about the appearance of the place, but I will have the departmental officers look into the matter and see whether some improvement cannot be made.
Did the minister say he had been informed that no complaints had been lodged? Complaints were lodged some days ago.

I have no knowledge of any, but perhaps I have overlooked the letter. I will search my files and see if a complaint has been received. However, we shall be very glad to look into the subject and see if some improvement cannot be made.

Item agreed to.
Administration of the Transport Act.
400. Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada-administration, maintenance and operation, $275,200.
Has Commissioner Stoncman been reappointed, and what is his salary?

Commissioner Stoneman's
term was completed in March of this year, and he was reappointed for a further period of ten years.

Supply-Transport-Railway Service

I suppose it is too late to protest, but I for one do protest. If there is a man in whom the people are disappointed it is this gentleman. Before he was appointed to this office he was a great believer in the equalization of freight rates, and at the time of his appointment it was thought he would give some consideration to the question of removing some of the obstacles with which we have had to contend. But he was the biggest obstacle we have ever had in British Columbia. As I say, I assume it is too late to protest now, but I am voicing the sentiments of many people when I say that he has disappointed us in his discharge of the trust reposed in him. I would make that statement outside the house too.

I can say for Commissioner Stoneman that for the four years that I have been associated with him I have found him exceedingly capable and conscientious, and any action he has taken has been from a sense of duty and fairness.

I think it would be a serious mistake to establish in this house the precedent that a person holding a public office of trust of this kind should be subject to the charge that he is or has been guilty of a breach of that trust. I have no brief for Mr. Stoneman nor do I know him personally at all, or in a friendly way, but I do know him as a public officer. I have been interested in cases that have gone before the board of railway commissioners during the years that he has been there, and while I can, say that he did not take the side of the case to which I was myself favourable, at the same time I am of opinion that Mr. Stoneman, as a railway commissioner, is a man with a high sense of public duty. I believe that he has served his country well and deserves commendation rather than condemnation. The fact that a person in a judicial or semi-judicial position renders decisions that we do not like is no reason why he should be held up to public contempt in this house. Personally I should not like this opportunity to pass without protesting against that method of intimidating persons holding public office. There is a way of dealing with such persons. Any member of the judiciary is subject to impeachment before this house, and in my experience here I have known of one judge having been impeached. Fortunately I do not recall any more. The high standing of our judiciary-and this is a semi-judicial position-is maintained because its members are not subject to public influence and political or public attack, provided they discharge their
duties. If they do not discharge their duties and are false to their trust they are subject to impeachment in the house in a proper manner.

The hon. gentleman is as much entitled to his views as I am to mine. It could not be from any motive of intimidation that I have made these remarks, because if that were so, the remarks would have been made last year before he was reappointed for a term of ten years. I do not believe the hon. member has done what I did. I had personal experience before the board and I know whereof I speak.

Item agreed to.
Railway service.
437. Railway grade crossing fund-amount to be placed to the credit of the railway grade crossing fund, and to be applied by the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada pursuant to, and within the limitations of, the provisions of section 262. of the Railway Act, as enacted by chapter 43 of the statutes of Canada, 1928, and amended by chapter 54 of the statutes of Canada, 1929, $500,000.
Has any progress been made in regard to the Jones avenue crossing in Toronto?

I have not yet had a report from the board, but I had a letter from the city some weeks ago offering to pay a proportion of the cost. It seemed reasonable to me, and I rather fancy it will be proceeded with this year, although the railway board, which has the allocation of the projects, has not yet sent it forward for action by the government.

Each year on these estimates, and elsewhere, I have brought up this matter and discussed it at considerable length. There are in the east end of the city three grade crossings-really four-which are a serious menace to safety and to traffic. I know from previous conversations with the minister and from questions I have asked, that the allocations are in the hands of the board, but there is a general feeling that the Jones avenue crossing is the first one that should be proceeded with. If any work were done now and carried to a successful conclusion it would be of considerable benefit to the east end of the city.

There is an increase of $200,000 in this item. One is bound to approve such an increased appropriation when it does away with as many level crossings as possible. How much was spent last year in the elimination of crossings?

Up to last year the contribution to grade crossings was a statutory matter fixed at $200,000, and we appropriated $300,000

Supply-Transport-Railway Service
in the main estimates, bringing the total up to $500,000 for that item and then increased it by a vote of $1,000,000 for the works program for special work, so that the total vote last year was $1,500,000. The total vote this year is the same, except that there is no statutory authority for $200,000, because statutory authority expired on March 31, 1939. It was practically all committed. Applications are filled with a reasonable distribution among the various provinces, but generally it is a matter of first come, first served, provided the projects are considered worth while by the board of railway commissioners.

I am sure the minister will realize the importance of eliminating some of the existing crossings. This year, having regard especially to increased unemployment throughout the dominion and not in any particular centre, I should like to know whether any plans have been formulated so far to carry forward some of these projects which perhaps would not be considered were it not for the fact that they were designed to give employment. These works, contributing as they do to public safety and public convenience, are exceedingly valuable as part of a public works program. They are designed not only for the relief of unemployment as palliative measures, but to serve an eminently useful public purpose. Are any plans in contemplation in this regard in view of the increased unemployment?

It is impossible to allocate funds to projects until the money is voted, and to date we have only twenty per cent voted. There have been two or three projects passed on to the government on the recommendation of the board of transport commissioners. From what I know of the general situation, the board is giving serious consideration to the Jones avenue project, but the city's offer of participation dates back only perhaps two months, and plans and tenders have to be called for, so it is not surprising that this particular project is not before the government yet. However, now that the money is available, the board will ask the government to allocate it rapidly.

The minister appreciates, of course, .that while my first question was of a particular nature in regard to the Jones avenue crossing in Toronto, the last remarks were of a general nature applying to the whole country.

The minister stated that there was $1,500,000 to be appropriated this year for grade crossing elimination. This vote is for $500,000. Under what vote is the other $1,000,000?
[Mr. Howe.)
Special supplementaries. We shall come to that presently.

Item agreed to.
Kailway service.
*439. Hudson Bay railway-construction and improvements-capital, $25,000.

I do not think there is enough attention given to the Hudson Bay railway project. I understand the Canadian National have the running rights, and the harbour is controlled by the national harbours board. It seems to me that those who have control of the shipping, the railway and the harbour are not trying to get the business that could be got for that railway and harbour. I think the Churchill harbour should be under a separate board composed of representatives from the three prairie provinces and possibly another person named by the department or the minister. But more attention should be given to getting more business, incoming as well as outgoing, for that port. It could be put on a basis where it would carry itself and be of much greater advantage to western Canada than it is.

There is no lack of attention to Churchill. As my hon. friend is familiar with the grain business, he knows there are conditions which make it possible to move grain through Churchill and conditions which make it impossible. In the early months of last year it was impossible to move grain through Churchill owing to the premiums on the Fort William route. However, we did one thing last year which has never been done before, we moved a million bushels of the crop of 1938-39 through the port of Churchill after the crop was harvested. This is the first time that movement has ever taken place, which is most encouraging. The elevator at the moment is filled with grain; certain grain is being held in country elevators for movement through Churchill, and I think we have every prospect of a satisfactory season this coming summer.
As for the turning of the port over to someone else, after all the government have an investment of some $51,000,000 there altogether, I think, in the railway and terminal; if my hon. friend finds anyone who would care to lease it we would let him have it at a reasonable price. But failing that, I think he had better let the department that constructed the port continue to operate it.
I do not think there is sufficient effort made to get incoming business.

How does my hon. friend know that? The department has done everything it can do.

Supply-Transport-Travel Bureau
I think I know on pretty good authority. Last year, for instance, I understand a company was ready to bring in binder twine but could not get storage facilities.
That is absolutely incorrect; no boat was scheduled for movement into Churchill.
But before, the boat was put on, the company that was getting the business in wanted to know first if it would have storage facilities, and I understand they were refused.
That is not correct.
Binder twine is not a perishable article-

Will my hon. friend accept my statement, from intimate knowledge of the situation, that his statement is absolutely incorrect? No binder twine was refused storage at Churchill last year; no binder twine moved to Churchill for the reason that no boat came to Churchill from Great Britain because they could not get a return cargo on account of there being no grain in Churchill.
Then I suggest that the government close the port, if no more effort is made than is being made at the present time by the Department of Transport to get business for it.

The province of Saskatchewan keep a man exclusively for the purpose of getting business for Churchill, and I assume he is doing his best. Will my hon friend suggest that that is wasted effort, or is that excellent work while our work is bad?
I think those interested would cooperate with the department if they could get cooperation for business.
If my hon. friend would confine himself to something he knows instead of what he picks up on the street we would get along better in this house.
I do not pick it up on the street. If we had a proper place we could produce the evidence.
Produce it now.
We never had a chance
I do not see any advantage in shipping the wheat through Churchill instead of Fort William. Fort William is a better route and safer.

Item agreed to.
Canadian travel bureau service.
445. To assist in promoting tourist business in Canada, $315,000.

I notice there is an increase of $65,000 in this item. I believe it could be many times such an increase and return many fold in benefits to Canada. I do not think there is any other country employing in its service any more efficient men in such publicity work than our own Mr. Dolan. He has done a most excellent piece of work, and has recently been singularly honoured in an international conference in the United States. The contribution he has already made to Canada is outstanding, and whereas I fully subscribe to the amount that has been spent in previous years, last year $250,000, we must recognize that the tourist trade, as I have already said on a previous occasion this session, is one of the most valuable we have. And anyone who has been in business, as the minister himself has been, knows the value of advertising. Advertising is most effective when it is not only efficiently done but when it has the right type of product to sell. I am confident that this year particularly, with the visit of their majesties not only to Canada but to the United States, Canada is more before the world now than she has been for many years. While one would not for a moment suggest that the visit of their majesties is regarded as advertising- do not think that for a moment-yet we must realize that with their majesties going to the United States this year from Canada, Canada will become of peculiar interest to the United States in the course of the next two or three weeks. The holiday season starts very soon. We could spend a substantial sum of money in the United States in advertising with great benefit not only to the country as a whole but to the individual citizens of the country. Few countries can boast of the natural advantages that we have here from the point of view of a playground and facilities for outdoor enjoyments of all sorts and of natural beauty. Travelling from the Atlantic to the Pacific one finds everywhere an outdoor paradise. There are routes such as the road round Gaspe, some in the maritimes, in parts of Quebec and Ontario, across the prairies and in British Columbia with which there are no others to compare.
Certainly there are one or two in Quebec to which that statement might apply.

I spoke of Quebec, and one might say through Sheilbrooke particularly.

Supply-Transport-Travel Bureau
The pamphlet that was prepared by the bureau this year under Mr. Dolan was exceedingly effective. I understand, however, from both observation and otherwise that the facilities at the disposal of the bureau at the present time are, to say the least, somewhat inadequate. The minister has probably noticed the handicaps under which the branch is working. They are sending out thousands of pieces of literature daily from a shipping room which is utterly unsuitable to the type of work being done. The department, itself, is on one floor of the building and the shipping room is in the basement. There is a great deal of confusion and waste of time between the two. Working conditions there are unsatisfactory.
But in spite of all these handicaps, Mr. Dolan and his staff are doing a good piece of work. I rise to speak briefly on the item, earnestly to urge upon the minister, first, that he take steps to provide his department with adequate and efficient facilities and, second, that he give earnest consideration to an extension of this item, so that we may take full advantage this summer of the unusual opportunities offered to us, and give the people not only in the United State but in other countries the inspiration to come to Canada to enjoy a holiday in the finest country of the world.

It is difficult to know what would 'be a proper amount to spend under this item. Originally the purpose was to set up an office to coordinate the efforts being made by the different provinces and by the railway systems in Canada. I think we are doing that to a considerable extent, and we are acting as a clearing house for general information. It is the duty of the department not to advertise any particular part of Canada, but to advertise the country as a whole, and to direct inquiries to the particular agency best suited to handle them. From year to year the volume of inquiries has increased tremendously. I believe that to-day we are serving a considerable part of the tourist public.
The minister will understand that I am not criticizing what has been done to date.

I understand that. I was speaking more particularly of the size of the vote. It is larger this year, to provide for the opening of an office in New York city. This is being tried somewhat as an experiment. It is thought that the fair gives adequate reason for opening an office in that city, and if the results are satisfactory, and if a fair volume of business goes through the office,

we will perhaps open offices in Chicago and San Francisco, although a decision in regard to those two cities has not as yet been made.
The vote is supplemented this year by one in the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce, involving special expenditures at the fair. We are making a real effort to attract tourists on the fair grounds, as well as from the uptown office. After studying this matter, my view is that the best course is to proceed gradually, and to make sure that each step is warranted before we make expenditures which may not be justified.
Did the minister have in mind the improvement of office facilities, and so on?

We have given the bureau such accommodation as we can, with the room at our disposal. The whole department is rather cramped, and the bureau is in the same position. I doubt if we can work out any better arrangement until new accommodation is provided for the whole department.
What amount is being spent this year at the New York fair, and what is the estimated expenditure for the future, in the event of a permanent office being opened?

There is the sum of $65,000
included in the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce for expenditures on the fair grounds, and there is an increase of $65,000 in this estimate to provide for expenditures at the uptown office, and for other expenditures. In particular we are publishing a rather extensive booklet this year, and a number of other pieces of literature.

Does the bureau send
out the literature, or does it have the information respecting different points of interest throughout the country available in prominent places for distribution?

There is literature for distribution at the fair grounds and at the uptown office, but the greater part of it is sent out in reply to inquiries. We advertise in the newspapers inviting those who are interested to write the tourist bureau at Ottawa. When these inquiries are received, suitable literature is sent to the inquirers. The literature is forwarded to points outside Canada, we have not made the practice of distributing much of it within the country. I would refer particularly to a condition at Fairvale, New Brunswick, near the city of Saint John. I do not know whether this item is broad enough to cover the situation there. At that point the road runs under the railway ; the opening is very narrow, and I believe it is considered one of the most dangerous spots on the roads of New Brunswick. There have been many accidents at that point, and parents of school children do not permit them to go under the railway, because of the dangerous situation. The result is that on their way to school they pass over the railway. Possibly the minister will remember that a number of meetings were held in that community to discuss the situation, and I

believe a petition, was forwarded to the minister asking that something be done. Would a situation of that kind come under this vote, and if so, will anything be done this summer in an effort to eliminate the dangerous situation at Fairvale?

In other years the grade crossing vote could not apply unless it involved the elimination of a crossing. For that reason it would not apply to the project the hon. member has described, because the crossing is there and the necessary work would involve only an improvement. I might say that last year we broadened the scope of the million dollar vote so that we could take care of projects of the kind described. For that reason the application would be a proper one to bring before the board of transport commissioners. I have no recollection of having received an application in the matter; but in any event it should be sent to the board, rather than to me, because it has under its control the administration of the grade crossing fund. If the proper authorities will make application to the board of transport commissioners, or if they will renew an application already made, I am sure their representations will receive due consideration.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
